restatements.text: Reclassifies assault on an on-duty law enforcement officer as a felony and increases the maximum penalty to three years in prison.

findings.direction: toward longer maximum sentences and felony classification for assaulting a law enforcement officer
findings.quote: Assault on an on-duty law enforcement officer is a felony punishable by up to three years in prison.
findings.mechanism: It increases the maximum penalty for assaulting an on-duty law enforcement officer from one year in jail to three years in prison and classifies the offense as a felony.

analysis.answer: Current law punishes assault with up to one year in jail. This measure reclassifies assault specifically against an on-duty law enforcement officer as a felony and increases the maximum punishment to three years in prison.

Longer sentences will increase direct costs for the state prison system, while potentially shifting some short-term incarceration costs away from county jails. It also imposes higher opportunity costs on incarcerated individuals due to longer confinement and felony records.

State taxpayers will bear the increased costs of longer prison sentences. Law enforcement officers may benefit if the harsher penalty increases deterrence or incapacitates offenders for longer periods.
Prosecutors may use the threat of a felony charge and a potential three-year prison sentence to negotiate plea deals more effectively.

The measure addresses the perceived inadequacy of a one-year maximum penalty for assaulting a law enforcement officer. The mechanism of increasing the penalty and reclassifying it as a felony reaches this by allowing for longer periods of incarceration.
Prosecutors gain leverage and discretion, as the availability of a harsher felony charge provides more power in plea negotiations.
